CXMT 뒤에 있는 중국 공산당이 두렵다고 했다. 실제로 CXMT는 중국 공산당과 정부의 전폭적인 지원을 받으며 급성장했다. 반도체 국가 펀드의 대규모 투자를 받았고, 공장 부지도 무상이나 저가로 공급받았다. 이달 공개된 중국 AI 모델 ‘키미K3’는 저렴한 가격이 강점이다. ‘키미 쇼크’는 중국 AI 기술이 미국을 바짝 뒤쫓고 있음을 보여주는 동시에 AI 경쟁에서 반도체와 데이터센터, 전력의 가치가 보다 높아질 것임을 예고하고 있다. 성능이 좋고 저렴한 AI가 나오면 AI 모델을 돌리는 연산력 수요가 폭증한다. 그만큼 반도체와 전력 등 AI 인프라가 중요해질 것이다. 우리에겐 기회 요인도 있는 셈이다. 지난 주말 이재명 대통령은 미국에서 한·미 빅테크 기업 경영자와 만나 “대체 불가능한 글로벌 AI 공급망의 핵심 국가”로 도약하겠다고 선언했다. 한국과 미국 기업들은 총 9500억 달러(약 1390조원)에 달하는 초대형 협력을 추진하기로 했다. 이런 대형 호재에도 불구하고 어제 코스피는 1% 오르는 데 그쳤다. 시장에서는 ‘다크호스’ CXMT 상장이 글로벌 유동성을 블랙홀처럼 빨아들였기 때문으로 분석했다. 이 대통령은 미국에서의 ‘AI 선언’에 대해 “대한민국이 AI 시대를 이끄는 대체불가한 선도자로 도약하겠다는 국가적 출사표”라고 했다. ‘출사표(出師表)’라고 표현한 것처럼 정부는 전쟁에 임하는 각오로 우리 기업에 대한 정책적 지원과 전력망·산업용수 등 인프라 확충에 총력을 기울이기 바란다. 우리 기업인이 두렵다고 토로했던 ‘중국 공산당과의 경쟁’에 우리 기업만 외롭게 싸우게 하는 일은 없어야 한다.

editorial.titleTr: Editorial: China's Rise Threatening as AI Yields to Memory Chips
summaryTr: Chinese semiconductor company CXMT lists as top market cap, Korean firms express concern
China's AI technology catch-up accelerates with release of budget AI model 'Kimi K3'
Risk of isolation in competition with China without government policy support and infrastructure expansion
editorial.bodyTr: Chinese AI startup Moonshot AI recently shocked the world by unveiling the "Kimi K3," an artificial intelligence model that rivals those of American big tech companies. Now, China's memory semiconductor industry is accelerating its rise at a frightening pace. Chinese semiconductor company Changxin Memory Technologies (CXMT) made a splashing debut yesterday by topping China's stock market by market capitalization. CXMT plans to use the capital it secured to advance DRAM technology and expand production capacity. A top executive at a domestic memory company reportedly named CXMT as the most feared competitor not long ago, citing fear of the Chinese Communist Party backing CXMT. Indeed, CXMT has experienced explosive growth with full support from the Chinese Communist Party and government. It received massive investments from China's national semiconductor fund and was supplied factory land free of charge or at discounted rates. The "Kimi K3" AI model unveiled this month stands out for its low price point. The "Kimi shock" demonstrates that Chinese AI technology is closely pursuing that of the United States while simultaneously signaling that semiconductors, data centers, and power will gain even greater value in AI competition. When high-performance, affordable AI emerges, demand for computing power to run AI models skyrockets. Correspondingly, AI infrastructure like semiconductors and power will become increasingly critical. This presents an opportunity for us as well. Last weekend, President Lee Jae-myung declared in the United States that Korea would leap forward as "an indispensable core nation in the global AI supply chain," meeting with executives from Korean and American big tech firms. Korean and American companies agreed to pursue mega-scale cooperation totaling 950 billion dollars, roughly 1,390 trillion won. Despite such major positive developments, the KOSPI rose only 1 percent yesterday. Market analysts attributed this to the "dark horse" CXMT listing sucking up global liquidity like a black hole. Regarding his "AI declaration" in the United States, President Lee stated it was a "national declaration of intent for South Korea to leap forward as an irreplaceable leader driving the AI era." As he expressed it with the term "declaration of intent," the government should mobilize all its strength in policy support for our companies and infrastructure expansion including power grids and industrial water supplies, approaching this competition with the resolve of going to war. We must not allow our companies to fight alone in this "competition with the Chinese Communist Party" that our business leaders expressed fear of.

editorial.title: Fix the flaws
editorial.body: Revised labor law needs complementary legislation to restore legal certainty Hanwha Ocean Co. last week filed a lawsuit with the Seoul Administrative Court, challenging a National Labor Relations Commission ruling recognizing it as the employer of union members of an in-house subcontractor responsible for cafeteria and commuter bus services. This is the first case since the Yellow Envelope Act — the amended Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act — took effect in March in which a main contractor has challenged in court the commission's determination that it qualifies as an employer of subcontractors. Companies are expected to increasingly contest decisions by labor relations commissions widely regarded as pro-labor. Recent Supreme Court rulings in cases filed before the revised act went into force have also reinforced companies' resort to the courts by reaffirming that an employer has a duty to engage in collective bargaining only when it has a direct contractual relationship with the workers concerned. The legal battle over the Yellow Envelope Act has entered a second round, shifting from labor relations commissions to the courts. This lawsuit stems from inherent flaws in the revised Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act. The amended law has broadened the definition of an employer in vague terms to mean "a person who can substantially and concretely control and determine working conditions," further aggravating confusion at industrial workplaces. The problem is becoming even more serious as labor relations commissions, the first government bodies to determine whether a prime contractor qualifies as an employer of subcontracted workers, have been consistently siding with labor. The confusion extends beyond the recognition of a prime contractor as the employer of subcontractor union members. Employers fear that the scope of collective bargaining and strikes could be expanded without limit. Organized labor has been pressuring companies, emboldened by the revised law that has expanded the scope of labor negotiations and industrial actions to include even matters traditionally considered management prerogatives, such as wage systems and decisions on building or relocating factories. At a Cabinet meeting on July 21, President Lee Jae Myung made clear his view that demands by some major companies’ unions for a share of operating profits to be allocated as performance bonuses should not be subject to labor disputes, saying, “Personally, I think the case against allowing such demands as a legitimate cause for strikes is stronger.” That the president ordered a revision of the enforcement decree regarding demands for performance bonuses clearly demonstrates just how serious this issue is. Referring to a recent move by a Samsung Electronics union to seek labor-management negotiations by treating the construction of a semiconductor plant in the southwestern Jeolla area as an issue subject to industrial action, Lee expressed concern, saying, “The scope of issues that can become the subject of labor disputes appears to be expanding too broadly.” That is a judgment based on plain common sense. Lee ordered action, stating that the government must establish clear standards for labor disputes to minimize confusion, and the Ministry of Employment and Labor is reportedly working on related enforcement decrees and administrative interpretation guidelines. However, due to the inherent ambiguity of the regulations and the union-biased nature of labor relations commissions, even government guidelines are unlikely to clear up confusion at industrial workplaces. The revised law lacks provisions delegating detailed criteria, such as the scope of labor disputes, to a presidential decree, and generally, guidelines have no external legal binding force. Ultimately, unless the law is amended, companies are likely to turn to the courts to resolve conflicts surrounding its controversial provisions. If disputes are prolonged through labor commission reexaminations and subsequent court rulings, economic damage and confusion are bound to escalate. Labor circles are also pushing back, arguing that the legislative intent of the revised law cannot be diluted through administrative guidelines. Ultimately, the only way to quickly resolve the confusion and controversies arising from the revised act is to enact complementary legislation. summaryTr: 한국의 개정 노동법이 모호한 사용자 정의로 법적 혼란을 야기하며 법정 분쟁을 촉발하고 있다.
노동위원회가 노조를 우대하는 가운데 기업들이 판정에 이의를 제기하면서 분쟁이 전통적 범위를 넘어 확대되고 있다.
정부 지침만으로는 혼동을 해결할 수 없으며, 입법부는 명확하고 구속력 있는 기준으로 법을 개정해야 한다.
editorial.bodyTr:
한화오션이 지난주 서울행정법원에 소송을 제기했다. 구내식당과 통근버스 서비스를 담당하는 하청업체 노조원들의 사용자로 인정한 중앙노동위원회의 판정에 이의를 제기한 것이다. 3월 시행된 개정 노동조합 및 노동관계조정법, 이른바 '노란봉투법' 이후 원청업체가 노동위의 판정에 법원에서 이의를 제기한 것은 이번이 처음이다. 노동친화적이라는 평가를 받고 있는 노동위의 결정에 기업들이 법원에 호소하는 사례가 늘어날 것으로 예상된다. 개정법 시행 전에 제기된 사건들에 대한 최근 대법원 판결도 사용자가 근로자와 직접 계약관계를 맺을 때만 단체교섭 의무가 있다는 점을 재확인해 기업들의 법원 소송 제기를 부추기고 있다. 노란봉투법을 둘러싼 법적 분쟁이 2라운드에 들어섰다. 노동위에서 법원으로 무대가 옮겨진 것이다.

이번 소송은 개정 노동조합 및 노동관계조정법의 내재된 결함에서 비롯됐다. 개정법은 사용자의 정의를 "근로조건을 실질적이고 구체적으로 지배·결정할 수 있는 자"로 모호하게 확대했고, 산업 현장의 혼란을 더욱 심화시키고 있다. 원청업체가 하청근로자의 사용자인지 판단하는 첫 번째 정부 기구인 노동위가 일관되게 노동계 편에 서면서 문제는 더욱 심각해지고 있다.

혼란은 원청업체의 사용자 인정 문제를 넘어 확산되고 있다. 기업들은 단체교섭과 쟁의행위의 범위가 무한정 확대될 수 있다는 우려를 갖고 있다. 노동계는 개정법에 힘입어 임금체계와 공장 신축·이전 결정 같이 전통적으로 경영진의 권한으로 여겨지던 사항까지 노동교섭 및 쟁의행위의 대상에 포함시킬 수 있다는 자신감으로 기업들에 압박을 가하고 있다.

이준석 대통령은 7월 21일 국무회의에서 대형 기업들의 노조가 요구하는 경영성과금의 일부를 성과급으로 배분하는 것은 노동분쟁의 정당한 원인이 될 수 없다는 입장을 명확히 했다. "개인적으로는 그러한 요구를 정당한 쟁의행위의 원인으로 인정하기 어렵다는 쪽의 논리가 더 강하다"고 말한 것이다. 성과급 요구와 관련된 시행령 개정을 지시한 것은 이 문제의 심각성을 보여준다.

삼성전자 노조가 전남 서남부 반도체 공장 건설을 쟁의행위의 대상으로 삼아 노사교섭을 추진하려는 최근 움직임을 언급하며 대통령은 "쟁의행위의 대상이 될 수 있는 사항의 범위가 너무 광범위하게 확대되는 것 같다"고 우려를 표했다. 상식에 기반한 판단이다.

대통령은 정부가 쟁의행위의 범위에 대한 명확한 기준을 수립해 혼란을 최소화해야 한다고 지시했고, 고용노동부가 관련 시행령과 행정해석 지침을 마련 중인 것으로 알려졌다. 하지만 규정의 내재된 모호성과 노동위의 노조 편향성 때문에 정부 지침만으로는 산업 현장의 혼란을 해소하기 어렵다. 개정법이 대통령령으로 위임할 수 있는 상세한 기준, 예를 들어 쟁의행위의 범위 같은 것을 규정하지 않았고, 일반적으로 지침은 대외적 법적 구속력이 없기 때문이다. 결국 법 개정이 이루어지지 않으면 기업들은 논쟁이 되고 있는 조항들을 둘러싼 갈등을 해결하기 위해 계속 법원에 호소할 가능성이 높다. 노동위 재심과 후속 법원 판결을 거치면서 분쟁이 장기화되면 경제적 손실과 혼란은 확산될 수밖에 없다. 노동계도 개정법의 입법 의도를 행정지침으로 훼손할 수 없다고 반발하고 있다.

결국 개정법으로 인한 혼란과 논쟁을 신속하게 해결하는 유일한 방법은 보완 입법을 추진하는 것이다.

editorials.title: Fix the flaws
editorials.body: Revised labor law needs complementary legislation to restore legal certainty Hanwha Ocean Co. last week filed a lawsuit with the Seoul Administrative Court, challenging a National Labor Relations Commission ruling recognizing it as the employer of union members of an in-house subcontractor responsible for cafeteria and commuter bus services. This is the first case since the Yellow Envelope Act — the amended Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act — took effect in March in which a main contractor has challenged in court the commission's determination that it qualifies as an employer of subcontractors. Companies are expected to increasingly contest decisions by labor relations commissions widely regarded as pro-labor. Recent Supreme Court rulings in cases filed before the revised act went into force have also reinforced companies' resort to the courts by reaffirming that an employer has a duty to engage in collective bargaining only when it has a direct contractual relationship with the workers concerned. The legal battle over the Yellow Envelope Act has entered a second round, shifting from labor relations commissions to the courts. This lawsuit stems from inherent flaws in the revised Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act. The amended law has broadened the definition of an employer in vague terms to mean "a person who can substantially and concretely control and determine working conditions," further aggravating confusion at industrial workplaces. The problem is becoming even more serious as labor relations commissions, the first government bodies to determine whether a prime contractor qualifies as an employer of subcontracted workers, have been consistently siding with labor. The confusion extends beyond the recognition of a prime contractor as the employer of subcontractor union members. Employers fear that the scope of collective bargaining and strikes could be expanded without limit. Organized labor has been pressuring companies, emboldened by the revised law that has expanded the scope of labor negotiations and industrial actions to include even matters traditionally considered management prerogatives, such as wage systems and decisions on building or relocating factories. At a Cabinet meeting on July 21, President Lee Jae Myung made clear his view that demands by some major companies’ unions for a share of operating profits to be allocated as performance bonuses should not be subject to labor disputes, saying, “Personally, I think the case against allowing such demands as a legitimate cause for strikes is stronger.” That the president ordered a revision of the enforcement decree regarding demands for performance bonuses clearly demonstrates just how serious this issue is. Referring to a recent move by a Samsung Electronics union to seek labor-management negotiations by treating the construction of a semiconductor plant in the southwestern Jeolla area as an issue subject to industrial action, Lee expressed concern, saying, “The scope of issues that can become the subject of labor disputes appears to be expanding too broadly.” That is a judgment based on plain common sense. Lee ordered action, stating that the government must establish clear standards for labor disputes to minimize confusion, and the Ministry of Employment and Labor is reportedly working on related enforcement decrees and administrative interpretation guidelines. However, due to the inherent ambiguity of the regulations and the union-biased nature of labor relations commissions, even government guidelines are unlikely to clear up confusion at industrial workplaces. The revised law lacks provisions delegating detailed criteria, such as the scope of labor disputes, to a presidential decree, and generally, guidelines have no external legal binding force. Ultimately, unless the law is amended, companies are likely to turn to the courts to resolve conflicts surrounding its controversial provisions. If disputes are prolonged through labor commission reexaminations and subsequent court rulings, economic damage and confusion are bound to escalate. Labor circles are also pushing back, arguing that the legislative intent of the revised law cannot be diluted through administrative guidelines. Ultimately, the only way to quickly resolve the confusion and controversies arising from the revised act is to enact complementary legislation. editorials.titleTr: Editorial: Stop the Trick of Shrinking Welfare by Lowering the Standard Median Income
summaryTr: The government will finalize the method for calculating the median income standard for next year by the end of this month.
The median income standard is a key criterion for determining eligibility in approximately 80 welfare programs.
Welfare benefits are being reduced due to arbitrary decisions by the Central Livelihood Security Committee.
editorials.bodyTr:
The government plans to finalize the calculation method for the "standard median income" to be applied from next year by the end of this month. The standard median income serves as the basis for determining beneficiaries and benefit amounts across approximately 80 welfare programs run by 14 different government departments, including the National Basic Livelihood Security System. Until now, the government-led Central Living Standards Committee has arbitrarily set the standard median income without sufficient deliberation, raising questions about fairness and transparency in the welfare system.

The process of determining the standard median income should be more transparent and evidence-based. It is necessary to establish objective standards and involve various stakeholders, including experts, civil society organizations, and beneficiaries, in the decision-making process. Furthermore, the calculation method should reflect the actual living conditions of the people and be adjusted appropriately based on economic indicators.

The standard median income directly affects the lives of vulnerable groups who rely on welfare benefits. Any arbitrary determination without proper deliberation could undermine the legitimacy of the welfare system and widen inequality. The government must approach this task with greater responsibility and openness.

We urge the government to announce the detailed calculation method well in advance and allow sufficient time for public review and feedback. Only through such transparent processes can we ensure that welfare policies truly serve their intended purpose of protecting those in need.
